title: The One With The Proposal (2)

jokes.text: You're with Chandler, a guy I really like. You say he's straight, I'll believe you.
jokes.setup: Richard is making a heartfelt, serious declaration of love to Monica while acknowledging she's with Chandler.
jokes.punchline: He undermines Chandler with a backhanded compliment implying he doubts Chandler's heterosexuality — a dig disguised as graciousness.
jokes.explanation: Sharp comedic aside buried in a melodramatic scene. The joke earns its laugh by subverting the earnest mood and landing a subtle insult at Chandler while Richard is ostensibly being generous. Good economy and timing, though it leans on a dated gay-joke trope that dulls the originality.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Monica, I love you. You mean everything to me. And Chandler... well, is he even interested in women?

jokes.text: Oh, my God. Why don't they put chairs back here?
jokes.setup: Richard has just told Monica he wants to marry her, have kids with her — an enormous emotional declaration.
jokes.punchline: Monica's response is to complain about the lack of chairs backstage, a completely mundane non-sequitur that deflects the emotional overwhelm.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional deflection joke. The setup is perfectly constructed — Richard delivers an emotionally loaded speech that demands a dramatic response, so Monica's hyper-mundane complaint about chairs is a brilliant comedic inversion. It's fully earned by the tension of the scene, and it's deeply character-specific: Monica, perpetually practical and over-organized, reaches for logistics when overwhelmed. This is what an 8 looks like — sharp, economical, surprising, character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Monica, I love you. I've always loved you. You mean everything to me, and I want to spend the rest of my life with—ow, my back. God, my back is killing me. Can we sit down?

jokes.text: What were you doing in Africa? / Working with blind kids.
jokes.setup: Richard says he spent six months in Africa trying to forget Monica after their last lunch — a romantic, self-sacrificial gesture.
jokes.punchline: He was working with blind kids, making his suffering look saintly and thus making it even harder for Monica to dismiss him, which is both moving and absurdly funny.
jokes.explanation: The joke works as a 'too good to be true' escalation — Richard keeps making himself more appealing and saintly just as Monica is trying to push him away. The punchline lands because it's so unfair to Monica. Solid construction, though it's a bit of a one-trick pony.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: I spent six months in Africa trying to forget you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, really?

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Yes. I was building schools and digging wells for villages that had never had clean water.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's... that's actually really sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: I know. It made me realize what's important in life.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So you got over me?

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Not even a little bit.

jokes.text: marriage is all he talks about... In fact, I'm the one making him wait.
jokes.setup: Richard challenges Monica to confirm Chandler is offering everything he is. Monica scrambles to defend Chandler.
jokes.punchline: She over-corrects so hard she claims she's the one holding back marriage — a blatant lie that the audience knows is false, since the whole plot is that Chandler won't commit.
jokes.explanation: Functional dramatic irony — the audience knows the truth and Monica's desperate overclaiming is funny. Not particularly original but well integrated into the scene's tension.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's in Africa helping blind kids? Oh come on! That's not fair! He's already impossibly handsome, he's successful, he's sophisticated... and now he's out there saving the world? He's becoming completely irresistible!

jokes.text: Because of the government.
jokes.setup: Richard presses Monica: why is SHE making Chandler wait? Monica has no answer. She says 'Why?' to stall.
jokes.punchline: "Because of the government." A completely nonsensical non-answer that's clearly improvised desperation.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The setup is perfectly engineered: Monica has talked herself into a corner with mounting pressure, and the audience is waiting for her to either confess or escape. 'Because of the government' is so random, so perfectly absurd, and so economical (four words) that it detonates instantly. It's character-specific — Monica's panic makes the nonsensical deflection believable. The lack of any follow-up makes it funnier still. High quotability. Genuinely exceptional economy.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Why are you making Chandler wait for marriage?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, if we get married before the government says it's okay, they can take away our tax exemptions and give them to the Presbyterians!

jokes.text: Two best friends in love. How often does that happen? / Not that often. / No. / I'm so happy for them. / Me too. So happy for them. / I'm so happy and not at all jealous. / Oh, no! God, definitely not jealous.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are congratulating each other on Monica and Chandler's engagement, talking up how happy they are.
jokes.punchline: The mutual overclaiming of happiness rapidly escalates until both are protesting too much — the irony that both are jealous is completely transparent.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom dramatic irony where overclaiming reveals the truth. Works well as a scene-setter and character moment. Not particularly original but efficiently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm so happy for you guys!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, it's not fair. Why does Monica get to be happy? I'm supposed to be the pretty one with the good life.

jokes.text: I'm probably 98 percent happy and maybe 2 percent jealous. / What's 2 percent? That's nothing. / Totally. / I'm like 90-10. / Yeah. Me too.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel have been insisting they're not jealous. Now they're quantifying their jealousy.
jokes.punchline: The numbers slide from 98/2 to 90/10 in seconds — both characters are clearly lying and the rapid recalibration is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Nicely structured escalation that pays off the previous joke. The percentage breakdown device is clever and the rapid deterioration from 98% to 90% lands well. Builds well on the prior joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm 87% sure I want to get married. 9% terrified. 3% wondering if I left the stove on. And 1% thinking about that guy from the coffee place.

jokes.text: No. But you know who was looking for you? Tennille.
jokes.setup: Joey/Phoebe-era character asks if anyone has seen Chandler. The other person gives a roundabout non-answer.
jokes.punchline: "Tennille" — a name drop that arrives out of nowhere, referencing Captain & Tennille in context of the boat captain costume gag that follows.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the boat captain visual gag that follows. The Tennille reference is a bit of a throwaway but earns rewatch bonus as it foreshadows Joey's costume. Weak on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, 2%? That's nothing! I mean, you're barely jealous at all. You're like, the least jealous person I know. It's actually kind of inspiring how you're just totally fine with everything.

jokes.text: Look at pigs. Let's take a second here and look at pigs. Pigs don't mate for life. A pig can have 100 sexual partners in a lifetime. And that's just an ordinary pig, not even a pig that's good at sports.
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to talk a woman out of wanting marriage by arguing marriage is unnatural, citing animal behavior.
jokes.punchline: "And that's just an ordinary pig, not even a pig that's good at sports." The escalation from vaguely coherent animal-behavior argument to completely deranged qualifier is perfect Joey.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The joke is built in layers: the absurdity of using pig behavior to argue against marriage is funny, then escalated brilliantly by the sports qualifier, which makes no logical sense but is completely coherent as Joey logic. 'Not even a pig that's good at sports' is the kind of line that gets quoted for decades. Near-perfect character integration — only Joey would think this is a persuasive argument. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality; the character specificity pushes it slightly higher.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I was like 80% jealous.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I was 90% jealous!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I wanted to claw your face off!

jokes.text: Is this some new strategy? Why don't you put down your copy of The Rules, huh, man-trap?
jokes.setup: The woman Joey is seeing reacts badly to his anti-marriage speech. Joey, oblivious to his own fault, turns it back on her.
jokes.punchline: He accuses her of running a strategy from "The Rules" and calls her a "man-trap" — completely inverting the situation where HE was just mansplaining pig sex.
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-serving obliviousness is well-deployed here. The term 'man-trap' and the reference to 'The Rules' (a real 1990s dating book) is period-specific and funny in context. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Have you guys seen Chandler?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, um... Marcus? Have you seen Marcus?

jokes.text: It's okay. I got a plan.
jokes.setup: Joey's girlfriend has just walked out on him. He looks devastated.
jokes.punchline: His immediate pivot to confident scheming — 'I got a plan' — delivered with complete sincerity despite having no plan whatsoever, is pure Joey.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey confidence-without-substance. Brief but effective. The scene-cut presumably reveals what the 'plan' is (the backup pact), which retroactively makes the line funnier. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look, marriage is unnatural. Humans aren't meant to be with one person forever.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know who has it figured out? Pigs. Pigs don't get married. Pigs just... do their thing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We should be more like pigs. It's science.

jokes.text: That's what makes it so easy to be 80 percent happy for Monica and Chandler.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are reassuring each other they'll find love. Ross is being optimistic.
jokes.punchline: The 'percent happy' metric from the earlier scene reappears, but now Ross has degraded from 90% to 80% — the jealousy is winning.
jokes.explanation: Effective callback that continues the running percentage joke. The drift from 90 to 80 is a nice beat — it's getting worse for Ross despite everything. Clean and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: If a pig were athletic, he'd get more action.

jokes.text: Some people make deals with a friend. Like if neither of them are married by 40, they marry each other. / You mean a backup? / Exactly. / Yeah, yeah. I've got that.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are lamenting being single while friends get engaged.
jokes.punchline: Rachel casually reveals she already has a backup spouse deal locked in, deflating the idea before it can go anywhere.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the larger backup-spouse chaos subplot. Works as functional comedy but is more of a premise-establisher than a standalone joke. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You need to get married, Joey. You're not getting any younger.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Are you trying to manipulate me? Because that's what my ex-girlfriends do!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm not manipulating you, I'm just saying—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, I know manipulation when I see it. The guilt trips, the pressure about my age... that's textbook stuff!

jokes.text: Joey? Are you serious? / Yeah. / Yeah, I locked him in years ago.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks who Phoebe's backup is, expecting a reasonable answer.
jokes.punchline: Joey — which surprises Rachel because Joey is so comically ill-suited for a serious life commitment.
jokes.explanation: Joey as the least viable backup husband is an inherently funny concept. The reveal lands but doesn't go anywhere especially surprising yet — that's the next joke's job.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: My jealousy percentage has increased even more.

jokes.text: Yep. We shook on it. Yeah. But believe me, that is not how he wanted to seal the deal.
jokes.setup: Phoebe confirms she and Joey made a deal and they shook on it.
jokes.punchline: "That is not how he wanted to seal the deal" — implying Joey pushed for something sexual, delivered with Phoebe's characteristic breezy candor.
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-timed innuendo. The punchline earns its laugh through Phoebe's matter-of-fact delivery of something scandalous. Good economy and character integration — this is completely Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I have Joey as my backup. You know, in case I get to like 40 and I'm not married, we're getting married.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, we made a pact. It's all very official. I have it notarized.

jokes.text: [PURRS]
jokes.setup: Phoebe is recounting Joey's exact words when he tried to seal the backup deal.
jokes.punchline: Instead of words, she purrs — implying Joey's proposal was essentially animal-level seduction.
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff. After the innuendo setup, the purr is maximally economical — one sound replaces a paragraph of description and is funnier than anything Phoebe could have said. The physical delivery (Phoebe doing her best Joey impression) adds visual comedy. The rewatch bonus is for catching the layered implication on first watch vs. subsequent viewings.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So we're really doing this? We're gonna get married if we're both still single at 40?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, we shook on it. It's official.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I think we should seal it with a kiss.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A kiss? I was thinking something a little more... binding.

jokes.text: Hey, Monica. Have you seen Rachel? Or a mirror?
jokes.setup: Joey enters wearing a full captain's uniform/hat — a ridiculous costume we now see for the first time.
jokes.punchline: He asks Monica if she's seen a mirror, implying he wants to admire himself — his vanity and obliviousness to how absurd he looks is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The captain costume is a visual comedy anchor for Joey's subplot. 'Or a mirror?' is a nice self-aggrandizing touch. The Tennille callback adds a rewatch layer.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Monica, have you seen Rachel?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, I haven't. Why?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Or a mirror.

jokes.text: It's for my boat. Cool, huh? / Yeah, it's great. / What's the matter? Talk to the captain.
jokes.setup: Joey is wearing an elaborate captain's uniform. Someone is visibly upset.
jokes.punchline: Joey's response to genuine emotional distress is to stay in character as 'the captain' and offer to dispense wisdom — completely unaware of how unhelpful this is.
jokes.explanation: 'Talk to the captain' is a memorable line that works both as visual comedy (the costume) and character comedy (Joey staying in bit while someone is upset). The juxtaposition of the silly costume with Rachel's genuine emotional crisis is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, check it out! I got this mirror for my boat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you don't have a boat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, but when I do, I'm gonna need this. It's for seeing behind the boat when you're backing up.

jokes.text: Chandler loves marriage! / You just told me he hates marriage! That he's a complex fellow who's unlikely to take a wife! That he's against marriage and always will be! / You got that from what I said?
jokes.setup: Joey has been carefully lying to Monica/Rachel about Chandler's feelings on marriage. When he hears Richard proposed, he panics and reveals the truth.
jokes.punchline: Joey's indignant 'You got that from what I said?' — as if Rachel misheard his series of explicit statements — is perfect oblivious comedy.
jokes.explanation: Superb callback payoff. Joey's earlier lies are now recited back to him verbatim, and his response — acting as if he was misunderstood — is a perfect expression of his character. The structure is excellent: the list of his own statements followed by the disbelieving non-denial is classically constructed comedy. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor; the character specificity and callback structure elevate it. 'You got that from what I said?' has genuine quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey Monica, what's wrong? You look upset.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm fine, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No you're not. But don't worry, Captain Joey is here to help.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Captain? Since when are you a captain?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Since I got my boat! I'm Captain Joey now.

jokes.text: So, what do you say we make a pact? If you and I are both single by 40, we get married. I mean, we know each other, we like each other...we've already slept together, so there'll be no surprises there. No, like, 'What's that?'
jokes.setup: Ross is making what sounds like a romantic proposal to Rachel — a sweet backup-spouse offer.
jokes.punchline: He undermines the romance by explicitly mentioning they've already slept together as a practical point, then makes it worse by adding a voice — "What's that?" — implying a hypothetical shock at an undisclosed physical attribute.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ross oversharing — turning a potentially romantic moment into an awkward practical inventory. The "What's that?" voice is the kicker that takes it from mildly funny to properly cringeworthy. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The man doth protest too much, methinks. He speaketh of marriage as one speaketh of root canal.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. I already have one. / Who? / Phoebe. / Phoebe? / But she just said Joey is her backup.
jokes.setup: Ross pitches the backup spouse idea to Rachel as if it's new and special.
jokes.punchline: Rachel already has one — and it's Phoebe, who Ross thought had a deal with him, initiating the backup chaos.
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the Phoebe chaos. Functions well as a gear-change into the farcical subplot. Not strong on its own but efficiently moves the plot.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler hates marriage! He's not gonna want to get married!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? He proposed to me!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh... oh no. Oh no no no. I didn't know that part. Forget everything I said. Chandler loves marriage! He's crazy about marriage!

jokes.text: That's impossible. We have had a deal for years. We shook on it. Although, believe me, she wanted to do a lot more than that.
jokes.setup: Ross is outraged to learn Phoebe has Joey as a backup when he thought he had a deal with Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: He mirrors Phoebe's earlier line about Joey — but reversed — implying Phoebe wanted to seal the deal with Ross sexually too, making Phoebe the promiscuous one in both tellings.
jokes.explanation: Excellent mirror callback — the structure of the joke is identical to Phoebe's earlier line about Joey, but applied to Ross, which retroactively reframes Phoebe as an equal-opportunity seducer. The parallel construction is well-crafted and the comedic escalation of Phoebe's character is a payoff that rewards attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You said marriage is a death trap, it's the end of freedom and adventure, and by the way, you're not even sure he likes women!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So that's not exactly a ringing endorsement!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I was just making conversation!

jokes.text: Where have you been? / I was making a coconut phone with the Professor.
jokes.setup: Ross urgently needs Joey's help with the Monica crisis.
jokes.punchline: Joey's nonchalant explanation — he was making a coconut phone with 'the Professor' — is a Gilligan's Island reference that also reveals he's been playing make-believe in his captain costume.
jokes.explanation: Delightful absurdist callback. The Gilligan's Island reference is a perfect extension of the captain costume bit — Joey has apparently been living out a fantasy rather than helping in a crisis. The specificity of 'coconut phone with the Professor' is what elevates this above a simple 'I was busy' joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, there would be no surprises if we got married. I mean, we've already slept together.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's not really a surprise anymore.

jokes.text: Stop messing with her! / And I would have if these damn boat shoes wouldn't keep flying off!
jokes.setup: Ross yells at Joey for not stopping the Monica-Richard situation.
jokes.punchline: Joey defends himself by complaining his boat shoes keep flying off, implying he was literally chasing someone in costume footwear.
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy built on the costume gag. The specificity of 'boat shoes flying off' is funnier than a generic physical excuse. Joey's indignant tone sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We shook hands on it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I thought you meant something else.

jokes.text: You know what I'll do? I'll go over there and kick his ass! Will you help me? / Look, us getting our asses kicked is not a solution.
jokes.setup: Chandler is panicking about Richard proposing to Monica and wants to fight Richard.
jokes.punchline: Ross's calm correction — 'us getting our asses kicked is not a solution' — immediately implies they would absolutely lose that fight, puncturing Chandler's tough-guy moment.
jokes.explanation: Ross's deadpan deflation of Chandler's bravado is well-timed. The humor lies in the implicit acknowledgment that Richard — a large, mustachioed doctor — would destroy them. Good character integration for both men.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Where have you been?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was on Gilligan's Island.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I got stuck there. The Professor couldn't fix the boat.

jokes.text: Dude! Dude! Dude! / That coconut phone might be good for the boat.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just delivered an urgent, emotional speech about proposing to Monica. Joey needs to contribute something to the moment.
jokes.punchline: Joey's contribution is to revisit the coconut phone idea for his boat. Completely tone-deaf to the drama.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey tone-deafness payoff. In the middle of an emotionally pivotal moment, Joey's mind wanders back to the coconut phone. The callback structure rewards attentive viewers and the brevity is perfect. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was trying to stop him, but these shoes have no traction!

jokes.text: I don't know why I'm here. / I didn't ask.
jokes.setup: Monica has shown up at Richard's apartment despite herself. She announces she doesn't know why she's there.
jokes.punchline: Richard's 'I didn't ask' — calm, undemanding, letting her off the hook — is both romantically generous and gently funny.
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfectly placed. Richard's response is simultaneously romantic and funny — his restraint is itself the joke. Maximum economy. The humor comes from the total lack of pressure where pressure would be expected.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Richard wants to marry Monica!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, Richard has a boat? I love boat shoes!

jokes.text: You still smoking cigars? / Uh... No, no. That's art.
jokes.setup: Monica notices what appears to be a cigar but Richard gave up smoking. He's clearly still smoking.
jokes.punchline: Richard insists it's 'art' — a transparent lie delivered with total composure.
jokes.explanation: Elegant small joke. Richard's instant, unashamed lie ('That's art') lands because Tom Selleck plays it utterly deadpan. The beat that follows — presumably Monica's disbelieving stare — makes it land harder. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! You can't fight him. The guy's like a hundred years old!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So? He'd kick your ass!

jokes.text: If it bothers you, I can put my art out.
jokes.setup: Richard has claimed the cigar is art. Monica seems uncomfortable.
jokes.punchline: He offers to 'put his art out' — which means extinguishing the cigar while maintaining the fiction that it's art. The double meaning is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Clever wordplay that extends the 'art' bit perfectly. 'Put my art out' as a phrase for extinguishing a cigar is elegant and Richard-specific — it has the refined, slightly arch wit that fits Tom Selleck's characterization of Richard. Good wordplay with minimal words.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, wait a minute. If I tie two of these coconut phones together, I could make a boat!

jokes.text: Since we broke up, do you ever think about me? / Actually, I thought about you a couple months ago. / Really? / Yeah, but it's because I had an eye exam, and I don't like my new eye doctor. / Who is it? / Edward Nevsky. / Yeah, he's no good.
jokes.setup: Richard asks Monica if she ever thinks about him in a romantic, vulnerable way.
jokes.punchline: Monica deflects into a mundane complaint about her eye doctor — and Richard, rather than being hurt, immediately validates the ophthalmology opinion.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured misdirection. The setup primes the audience for a romantic confession; the punchline is a mundane eye exam deflection; and then the second punchline — Richard's instant, sincere validation of 'yeah, he's no good' — adds an extra layer. The joke works on two levels: Monica's deflection and Richard's acceptance of the deflection while still pursuing her. Very well-crafted for a seemingly lightweight exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't know why I'm at your apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: I didn't ask for an explanation.

jokes.text: Do you ever think about me in... a non-eye-doctor way?
jokes.setup: The eye-doctor exchange has fully derailed Richard's romantic question.
jokes.punchline: Richard has to recalibrate his romantic inquiry to now specifically exclude ophthalmology — 'in a non-eye-doctor way' — which is an absurdly specific clarification.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. 'In a non-eye-doctor way' is a brilliantly specific phrase that earns high quotability. The fact that Richard has to now qualify 'romantically' as opposed to 'ophthalmologically' is a perfect extension of the bit. Economical and very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: I'm going to turn around now, and when I do, I want you to know that my eyes will be closed.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: I will keep them closed until you tell me you're completely inside and the door is shut.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Then I will open them, but only after counting to ten, so there's no possibility of any... awkwardness.

jokes.text: Phoebe, you picked Joey and Ross? You can't have two backups! / Of course I can. It's just good sense to back up your backup.
jokes.setup: Rachel discovers Phoebe has both Ross and Joey as backup spouses.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's completely reasonable-sounding logic — 'it's just good sense to back up your backup' — treats marriage like a computer file.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's tech-metaphor logic applied to romance is a great character beat. 'Back up your backup' has an almost corporate efficiency that clashes beautifully with the emotional subject matter. Well integrated into Phoebe's quirky-pragmatic worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'll have a...

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Cosmopolitan. You always order a Cosmopolitan.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How did you remember that?

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: I remember everything about you, Monica.

jokes.text: What are you complaining about? You were both aware of the situation.
jokes.setup: Ross and Joey both discover they're backups for Phoebe and both protest.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe dismisses their outrage as if she's being completely reasonable — she's the one wronged here.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's breezy dismissiveness is very on-brand. Works as a quick character beat. Not exceptional on its own but serves the escalating chaos well.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do you still smoke cigars?

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Well, I prefer to think of it as appreciating a fine art form. A cigar isn't merely tobacco—it's a carefully crafted expression of culture and refinement.

jokes.text: You can't have both. Pick one. / Pick me! / No, pick me!
jokes.setup: Phoebe must choose between Ross and Joey as her backup spouse.
jokes.punchline: Both men immediately lobby for themselves — eagerly competing to be a theoretical backup for a theoretical marriage 20+ years in the future.
jokes.explanation: Functional group comedy. The eagerness of two grown men competing to be a backup spouse is inherently funny, but the execution is straightforward. Serves the escalation of the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: It's not just extinguishing it, it's a deliberate artistic statement. The way the smoke dissipates into the air... it's like watching a Rothko fade into obscurity.

jokes.text: Well, let's see. Ross is a good father. But...Joey has a boat. This is hard.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is weighing Ross vs. Joey as a backup husband.
jokes.punchline: She weighs 'good father' against 'has a boat' as equivalent considerations — and genuinely finds it difficult.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Phoebe reasoning — the juxtaposition of 'good father' (meaningful) versus 'has a boat' (frivolous) as genuine competing considerations is perfect absurdist character comedy. The pause before 'Joey has a boat' and the follow-up 'this is hard' makes it land beautifully. High quotability and character integration. This is a highlight of the subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Do you ever think about me? Romantically?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, there was that one time...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But it was only because my gynecologist cancelled on me.

jokes.text: Remember my promise: If we get married, three times a week. / Oh, my God. Phoebe... / I'm talking about massages. [MOUTHS] No, I'm not.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to prevent Ross and Joey from withdrawing by sweetening the deal.
jokes.punchline: She says 'three times a week' (sexual implication), immediately clarifies 'I'm talking about massages' (innocent), then silently mouths to the camera 'No, I'm not' (absolutely not innocent).
jokes.explanation: Triple-layered misdirection: implication → denial → reversal-of-denial. The structure is almost perfectly executed — each beat flips the meaning one more time, and the final silent [MOUTHS] 'No, I'm not' to camera is a mini-meta moment that rewards the audience. The structure alone earns a 9. This is one of the best-constructed jokes in the episode and comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality and execution.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: My eye doctor is amazing. He's so good, he can tell what you're thinking just by looking in your eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: That's nothing. My eye doctor once told me I was going to die three weeks before it happened.

jokes.text: Pick one. / Left. / Thank you. / You're welcome.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has two napkins — one with 'Joey' and one with 'Ross' — and asks Rachel to pick one at random.
jokes.punchline: Rachel picks 'left' and Phoebe thanks her with absurd formality as if a grave decision has been correctly handled.
jokes.explanation: Light beat that works as procedural comedy. The formality of 'thank you / you're welcome' applied to picking a husband-napkin is quietly funny but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You guys are like my relationship RAID array. Ross, you're the mirror drive. Joey, you're the backup drive.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's not how relationships work.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh please. If Mike crashes, I need redundancy. You're both just sitting there waiting to be restored.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Did she just call me a backup drive?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And before you ask, no, I don't have a tertiary. That's what Monica's for.

jokes.text: Ross. / Joey. / We should just switch. / Absolutely.
jokes.setup: Phoebe gets Ross from the draw, Rachel gets Joey. Both got the 'wrong' one.
jokes.punchline: Without any discussion, both immediately agree to swap — which raises the question of why they went through the whole charade.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the napkin draw — the whole procedure was pointless because the result was immediately overridden by preference. The speed of the swap is the joke. Efficient and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, okay. So you guys are fighting about who gets to be with me if one of you dies? That's so sweet. But I have to tell you, I've already made my decision.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Who?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I'm going with Chandler. He's better at spooning and he lets me pick the movie.

jokes.text: Maybe someone with a license to practice medicine. Or a mustache.
jokes.setup: Monica is confiding to Richard about wanting a more mature partner.
jokes.punchline: She lists 'license to practice medicine' and 'mustache' as equivalent markers of maturity — directly describing Richard while pretending to speak generally.
jokes.explanation: Clever self-aware moment — Monica is essentially telling Richard she wants him, but framed as abstract requirements. 'Or a mustache' is the killer detail because it's so specific to Richard's iconic look. Good economy and genuine wit.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I have to choose between Ross and Joey as my backup husband? Well, Ross is a paleontologist with a child, so he's clearly experienced with parenting. But Joey has a boat!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Those are basically the same thing when you're picking a husband.

jokes.text: Coming to my work and telling me you love me, I want that! Talking about pig sex over lunch, I don't want that!
jokes.setup: Monica is laying out what she wants in a relationship — consciously or not comparing Richard and Chandler.
jokes.punchline: The callback to Joey's pig-sex lecture appears here — Monica's list of dealbreakers includes 'talking about pig sex over lunch,' anchoring the absurdist earlier comedy into emotional stakes.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural callback that earns its place because it bridges the comedic subplot (Joey's pig speech) and the emotional A-plot (Monica's relationship crisis). The callback recontextualizes the pig joke as actually meaningful within Monica's emotional arc. Well-constructed episode writing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You guys, you can't switch to Rachel! She's my friend!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Phoebe, we're just trying to save money on rent.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I'll make it worth your while. I promise you guys frequent sexual activity.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: With each other!

jokes.text: Take as much time as you want. Ten, 20 minutes, if you need it. / I'll be here. Not smoking.
jokes.setup: Monica needs time to think. Richard magnanimously offers her as much time as she needs.
jokes.punchline: He immediately quantifies 'as much time as you want' as ten or twenty minutes — classic manipulation dressed as patience. Then closes with 'not smoking' — a callback to the cigar bit.
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one: the gentle time-pressure of 'ten, 20 minutes' (barely disguised manipulation from a smooth operator) and the return of 'not smoking' as a final wink. Richard as a character works because his charm and manipulation are indistinguishable, and this line captures that perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? I give great massages!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, fine, I meant sex.

jokes.text: I'll be here. Not smoking.
jokes.setup: Richard tells Monica he'll wait for her while she thinks things over.
jokes.punchline: 'Not smoking' — a callback to the cigar/art joke from earlier, delivered as a small reassurance that doubles as a callback gag. Richard volunteering that he won't smoke implies the cigar is still very much on his mind.
jokes.explanation: Two-word callback. Richard adding 'not smoking' to 'I'll be here' implies the cigar situation from earlier is still alive and that he's making a small concession by not lighting up. The economy is exceptional. It also adds a touch of absurdity — in a romantic moment, he's pledging sobriety from his cigar/art.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm picking a name... Brad Pitt.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, it says 'Congratulations, you've won a lifetime supply of turtle wax.'

jokes.text: Chandler. / Where is she? / I'm not scared of you.
jokes.setup: Chandler bursts into Richard's apartment ready for a confrontation.
jokes.punchline: Richard's calm, amused 'I'm not scared of you' deflates Chandler's big entrance instantly and completely.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation. Chandler arrives in full antagonist mode; Richard's quiet confidence neuters him in four words. Works because it's true — Richard clearly would destroy Chandler — and Tom Selleck's delivery would be impeccable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, this is awkward. I got matched with someone completely wrong for me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, me too. This algorithm is terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? We should just switch.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay.

jokes.text: Scotch on the rocks with a twist, on a coaster.
jokes.setup: Chandler has stormed in looking for Monica and is ranting. Richard is meanwhile casually preparing drinks.
jokes.punchline: Richard already knows Chandler's drink order — revealing he pays attention and is unflustered — and the detail of 'on a coaster' adds a note of domestic refinement that makes Chandler look like an irresponsible guest.
jokes.explanation: The 'on a coaster' detail is Richard's character in a nutshell — he's the more grown-up option, literally. Nice character-contrast comedy. Works within the scene's larger dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I need to be with someone more mature.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Well, I'm 21 years older than you.

jokes.text: Nothing happened? Nothing? You didn't tell her you love her? / Well, all right, one thing happened.
jokes.setup: Chandler demands to know if anything happened between Richard and Monica.
jokes.punchline: Richard's calm correction — 'well, all right, one thing happened' — delivered with perfect understatement after Chandler's emphatic 'nothing?!' is classically timed.
jokes.explanation: Classic straight-man setup and understatement punchline. Richard's calm in the face of Chandler's hysteria is well-deployed. Good economy.

jokes.text: You made my girlfriend think!
jokes.setup: Chandler is cataloguing Richard's crimes: telling Monica he loves her, offering marriage.
jokes.punchline: His final accusation — 'you made my girlfriend think!' — frames independent thought as an act of aggression. The absurdity of treating Monica's deliberation as a harm done to Chandler is the joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode and arguably the episode's most quotable moment. 'You made my girlfriend think!' works on multiple levels: it's absurd (thinking = bad), it's character-revealing (Chandler's insecurity), it's perfectly economical (five words do everything), and it has the rhythm of a great comedy line. The structure is impeccable — escalation of accusations building to this as the climax. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in wit and economy; the originality and quotability push it higher. This is what an 8.5+ looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is so unfair! I can't believe this is happening to me!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is so unfair! This is so unfair!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is so unfair! This is so unfair! This is so unfair!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: THIS IS SO UNFAIR! THIS IS SO UNFAIR! THIS IS SO UNFAIR! THIS IS SO UNFAIR!

jokes.text: It was working till you showed up, you big tree.
jokes.setup: Chandler is explaining his plan to Richard, who correctly notes it worked very well.
jokes.punchline: 'You big tree' as an insult for a tall man — Chandler can't even muster a proper insult, landing on a description rather than an epithet.
jokes.explanation: 'You big tree' is a great Chandler insult because it's so ineffectual — he's angry but can't quite commit to a real insult, so he just describes Richard's height. Very character-specific for Chandler's particular brand of impotent verbal aggression.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Take as much time as you need to think about this.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: How does next Tuesday sound?

jokes.text: Did you get a ring? / No, I don't have a ring.
jokes.setup: Chandler has revealed he was going to propose tonight and shows Richard the ring. The tables have completely turned.
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks if Richard has a ring with what appears to be sincere temporary triumph; Richard's quiet admission that he doesn't is both defeat and dignity.
jokes.explanation: More of a dramatic beat with comedic undertones than a true joke. Works because of the reversal of power dynamics in the scene. Functional but not exceptional comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You told her you loved her?

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Well, yeah.

jokes.text: You know, Richard, you are a good guy. / I know. I hate that.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Richard have come to an unexpected understanding — Richard tells him to go get Monica.
jokes.punchline: Richard's 'I know. I hate that.' — accepting the compliment while being honest about how inconvenient his own decency is — is quietly perfect.
jokes.explanation: Four words — 'I know. I hate that.' — deliver character complexity, comedy, and pathos simultaneously. Richard acknowledging his own goodness with genuine frustration is both funny and moving. Perfect economy, perfect character integration. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor; the emotional layering and quotability place it solidly there. One of the most memorable exchanges in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe Richard keeps interfering! Every time Monica tries to make a decision, he's there telling her what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? At this point, I'm just grateful when Monica actually thinks for herself. That's like a positive outcome at this point.

jokes.text: Why didn't you tell her it was a plan? / I did! I told her everything. She wouldn't believe me.
jokes.setup: Ross wonders why Chandler didn't just explain the scheme.
jokes.punchline: He did — but it was such an implausible plan that Monica couldn't believe it, which is both funny and deeply Chandler.
jokes.explanation: Decent beat that underscores how badly the plan backfired. Chandler's particular brand of scheme-failure is on-brand. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My plan was working fine until Richard came along. The guy's so tall and imposing, he makes a sequoia look like a bonsai!

jokes.text: You wanted it to be a surprise.
jokes.setup: Chandler is devastated that his plan backfired. Ross is comforting him but also delivered the bad news.
jokes.punchline: Ross — presumably gesturing at the elaborate romantic setup Chandler arranged for the proposal — quietly points out that the surprise is working perfectly; Chandler just isn't there for the surprised part.
jokes.explanation: This line lands as a transition joke — from despair to the reveal of the candlelit proposal room. 'You wanted it to be a surprise' recontextualizes the disaster as actually being the setup for something beautiful, while still being funny. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? You're a good man. A really good man. And I hate you for it.

jokes.text: There's a reason why girls don't do this! / Okay, okay, okay.
jokes.setup: Monica has gotten down on one knee to propose to Chandler and is overwhelmed with emotion, unable to get through her speech.
jokes.punchline: Through tears she acknowledges that women typically don't do the proposing — the meta-awareness of her own collapse is very Monica.
jokes.explanation: Effective comedic relief in the most emotionally intense scene of the episode. Monica's self-aware aside while crying mid-proposal is very Monica — control-freak perfectionism colliding with overwhelming emotion. Good character integration and the comedic beat doesn't undermine the drama.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going down on one knee. Here we go...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh God, my back. Why do men do this? This is awful!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And how am I supposed to get back up? Do I just... roll?

jokes.text: I knew you were likely to take a wife!
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica just got engaged. The group rushes in to celebrate.
jokes.punchline: Joey triumphantly references his own earlier lie ('unlikely to take a wife') but inverts it — implying he always believed in Chandler, when he was actively undermining him an hour ago.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback. Joey's triumphant 'I knew you were likely to take a wife!' is funny on two levels: it uses the same archaic language as his earlier lie, and it completely rewrites history — he was doing everything to make Chandler look bad. The revisionist pride is classic Joey self-aggrandizement. The callback structure is elegant and the character integration is superb.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I just want to say, I always thought Chandler was unlikely to take a wife, and I was wrong.

jokes.text: Can we come in yet? We're dying out here!
jokes.setup: Joey (and presumably others) has been waiting outside for Chandler to propose. The engagement just happened.
jokes.punchline: Joey's dramatic 'We're dying out here!' — delivered with full commitment despite the fact he's been waiting mere minutes — is classic Joey hyperbole.
jokes.explanation: Light character beat. Joey's impatience framed as mortal suffering is on-brand. Functions as a good transition into the group celebration scene. Not exceptional on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Zero percent jealous.

jokes.text: This is the least jealous I've ever been!
jokes.setup: Everyone rushes in to celebrate the engagement. Rachel is genuinely happy.
jokes.punchline: Rachel callbacks to the entire jealousy-percentage running gag — but now inverts it, announcing with equal conviction that her jealousy is at an all-time low.
jokes.explanation: Excellent emotional callback that closes the jealousy running gag. The inversion works perfectly — where before it was overclaiming happiness while secretly jealous, now it's genuine happiness expressed in the same hyperbolic terms. Satisfying structural payoff to a thread that ran through the whole episode.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Where's Joey?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's on a date.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? He's missing our engagement party?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's not like he knew about it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Still! This is huge! We're all supposed to be here together!

jokes.text: Oh, no, wait! This is wrong! Ross isn't here! / He's done it three times. He knows what it's about! / GROUP: Yeah.
jokes.setup: In the joy of the engagement celebration, Phoebe remembers Ross is absent.
jokes.punchline: Monica/Joey/group immediately dismisses the concern — Ross has been engaged three times, he understands this moment implicitly and doesn't need to be there.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly dark. The group's immediate unanimous agreement that Ross's three failed engagements make him an honorary expert who needs no actual presence is both funny and a little mean, which makes it funnier. 'He's done it three times. He knows what it's about' is a great line — it treats his romantic failures as a credential. High quotability and strong character integration (everyone agreeing instantly is the joke).

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Where is Ross? He's missing the engagement celebration!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, he's probably at home practicing his vows. You know, so he can get them right this time. And the time after that. And the time after that.

insight: Proposal episode underdelivers at 59 — emotional weight outpaces comedy throughout.
